name: Saint Maarten
rule: Sint Maarten LVV plant controls still do not classify manufactured sencha. Separately, current Landsbesluit publieke gezondheid (AB 2017 no.33), article 4(2), confines food import notification to commercial use. Article 4(3) confines origin health certificates to commercial imports of dairy, fish, poultry/meat and baby food; plain tea is not listed. Its official explanatory note distinguishes personal from commercial use by presentation, packaging and quantity, without a passenger-only limitation. This narrows the unresolved issue to the separate plant-health classification rather than imposing commercial food paperwork on a 100g private parcel.
personalMailApplicability: The public-health notification/certificate duties are limited by intended commercial use, not by whether a seller was paid or by a traveler-only allowance. Treating a single 100g parcel intended for the recipient’s own consumption as personal follows the enacted scope and explanatory note. Independent LVV plant-product scope remains unverified.
authority: Sint Maarten LVV; Ministry of Public Health, Social Development and Labor; official local legislation register

name: Saint Vincent
rule: The linked Plant Protection Act is Act No. 16 of 2005 (assented 25 October 2005), not 2015. Section 2 includes manufactured products only where their nature or processing may create a pest-introduction/spread risk. Sections 10–11 provide import-permit and phytosanitary-document controls for designated articles; section 15 expressly covers postal interception. Ministry guidance includes personal-use plant material but does not classify finished sencha. The official general-food health guidance describes import inspection; it does not establish an origin health/free-sale certificate requirement for plain private tea. The Environmental Health Services Act 14/1991 provides handling, inspection and regulation-making powers without itself prescribing that certificate.
personalMailApplicability: Section 15 expressly covers the Postal Corporation and private postal operators. The ministry’s September 2019 guidance includes personal-use plant parts in permit controls. Neither establishes whether sealed steamed/dried sencha is a regulated manufactured product, nor a small personal-post waiver.

name: Turks and Caicos
rule: The Plant Health Ordinance defines manufactured products as regulated when processing/nature creates pest risk. The current 2024 Regulations cover postal regulated articles, home-consumption permits and documentation, but supply no explicit tea classification or processed-tea waiver. As enacted, Food and Drugs Ordinance 7/2016 section 3(2)(a) expressly excludes food imported for private consumption, so section 5 cannot be used as an unqualified private-import certificate duty. Section 1 requires a Gazette commencement notice, which was not independently recovered; the current Environmental Health website cites the 2016 Ordinance. Section 3(2)(d) also separates activities governed by Plant Health legislation.
personalMailApplicability: The enacted 2016 Food and Drugs Ordinance excludes private-consumption imports without a passenger-only qualifier, but its commencement notice remains unverified. Independent Plant Health rules expressly cover postal regulated articles; no manufactured-tea risk classification or agricultural waiver established.
